metaTitle: How to Check Contractor Reviews and References Properly
metaDescription: How Ontario homeowners can vet a contractor using Google Business Profile, BBB, HomeStars, and by actually calling two or three recent references.
h1: How to Check a Contractor's Reviews and References the Right Way
summary: A practical walkthrough of using Google reviews, BBB, HomeStars, and real reference calls to vet a contractor before you sign anything.
intro: Checking reviews is one of the easiest parts of hiring a contractor to do badly. A five-minute glance at a star rating tells you almost nothing on its own. This guide walks through the sources worth checking, what to actually look for in each one, and why calling references still matters even in an age of online reviews.

sections.heading: Start with Google Business Profile, but read past the star average

blocks.text: Google Business Profile reviews are usually the first thing homeowners see, and they are a reasonable starting point, but the overall star rating is the least useful number on the page. A contractor with 4.6 stars from 12 reviews and one with 4.6 stars from 200 reviews are not comparable businesses. Volume matters as much as the average.

items: Sort by most recent and check whether reviews are still coming in regularly, not clustered from years ago
Read a handful of the one and two star reviews specifically, and see how the business responded
Look for reviews that mention the actual type of work you need, a great review for a furnace tune-up says little about deck-building quality
Be cautious of a sudden spike of five-star reviews posted within days of each other, which can suggest a review-gating campaign

blocks.text: A business owner who replies calmly and specifically to a negative review, even a fair one, tells you more than a wall of five-star praise. Defensive or angry replies to criticism are worth noting.

sections.heading: Check the Better Business Bureau for complaint history

blocks.text: The Better Business Bureau, commonly known as BBB, is less about star ratings and more about formal complaint history and how a business handled disputes. A BBB profile shows whether complaints were filed, what they were about, and whether the business responded and resolved them. This is different information from a Google review and worth checking separately.
A pattern of unresolved complaints about the same issue, such as missed deadlines or incomplete work, is a stronger signal than a single bad review anywhere else.

Not every legitimate small contractor has a BBB profile, particularly newer or very small operations, so the absence of a listing is not automatically a red flag. What matters more is what shows up if a profile does exist.

HomeStars is built specifically around home renovation and trade work, which makes its reviews often more detailed than a general Google review. Homeowners on HomeStars tend to describe the actual scope of the job, the timeline, and whether the final price matched the quote, details that matter a great deal for planning a deck build, a concrete pour, or a roofing job.

items: Look at how many jobs of your specific type the contractor has documented
Check whether photos are included and whether they look like the same style of work you want
Note the score breakdown if available, not just the overall number, since categories like punctuality and clean-up vary independently

blocks.text: As with any review platform, cross-reference what you see on HomeStars against Google and BBB rather than relying on one source alone. A contractor who looks great on one platform and is absent or negative on another deserves a closer look before you proceed.

sections.heading: Ask for two or three recent references, and actually call them

blocks.text: Online reviews are useful, but they are also easy to game and impossible to ask follow-up questions of. A short phone call with a recent customer gives you something no review platform can: the chance to ask specific questions about your exact situation.

items.title: Ask for references from the last six months
items.text: Older references may reflect a business that has since changed crews, ownership, or quality standards.

items.title: Request a project similar to yours
items.text: A reference for a small repair does not tell you much if you are planning a full driveway replacement or a new deck.

items.title: Call, do not just email
items.text: A phone conversation lets you pick up on hesitation or tone that a written reply hides. Most people are candid on the phone if asked directly.

items.title: Ask about the parts reviews rarely cover
items.text: Did the crew show up when promised, was the final invoice close to the quote, and would they hire this contractor again for a different job.

blocks.text: A contractor who hesitates to give you any recent references, or only offers references from years ago, is telling you something. Most established businesses have satisfied recent customers who are willing to spend five minutes on the phone.

sections.heading: Spotting reviews that were not written by real customers

blocks.text: Fake or incentivized reviews are more common than most homeowners assume, and they tend to follow a recognizable pattern once you know what to look for. A cluster of reviews posted within the same short window, all with similar phrasing or an unusually generic tone, is worth extra scrutiny. Genuine reviews tend to mention specific details, a crew member's name, the exact service, or a particular part of the property, while fabricated ones often stay vague.

items: Watch for reviewer profiles with only one review ever posted, especially several appearing around the same date
Be skeptical of reviews that read like marketing copy rather than a homeowner's own words
Check whether the reviewer's profile has reviewed unrelated businesses in different cities, which can indicate a paid review service
A business with a mix of detailed positive and a few honest critical reviews generally reads as more credible than one with only glowing, uniform praise

blocks.text: None of this means you need to become a forensic investigator before hiring someone to seal your driveway. The point is simply to read with a slightly skeptical eye rather than taking the star average at face value, especially for a larger project like a deck build or a full concrete driveway replacement where the cost of a bad hire is significant.

sections.heading: Putting it together before you sign anything

blocks.text: None of these checks takes more than an hour combined, and that hour is small compared to the cost of a botched deck, a cracked driveway, or a roof that leaks the first winter. Treat review checking as a normal part of getting quotes, the same way you would compare prices, and be suspicious of any contractor who discourages you from doing it.

It also helps to see how a contractor is regarded within the trade itself, not just by past customers. Businesses recognized on /winners have generally been vetted beyond a simple star count, and browsing /resources for other hiring guides can round out your research before you commit to a project.

checklist: Read recent Google Business Profile reviews, not just the star average
Check how the business responds to negative reviews
Look up the contractor on BBB for complaint history
Cross-check HomeStars for trade-specific reviews and photos
Request two or three references from jobs completed in the last six months
Call references directly instead of relying on email
Ask references whether the final invoice matched the original quote
Compare findings across at least two review sources before deciding

faq.q: Is a high star rating on Google enough to trust a contractor?
faq.a: Not on its own. A high average from very few reviews tells you little, and star ratings can be manipulated. Read a sample of recent reviews, including negative ones, and see how the business responded before drawing conclusions.

faq.q: What if a contractor has no BBB profile at all?
faq.a: That is common for smaller or newer businesses and is not automatically a red flag. It simply means you should lean more heavily on Google, HomeStars, and direct references to form a picture.

faq.q: How many references should I ask for?
faq.a: Two or three recent ones, ideally from projects similar in scope to what you are planning, is usually enough to spot a pattern, whether that pattern is reassuring or concerning.

faq.q: What should I actually ask a reference on the phone?
faq.a: Ask whether the crew showed up on schedule, whether the final cost matched the quote, how clean-up was handled, and whether they would hire the same contractor again for a different project.
